sourceNote: Derived from the Jost Atlas of Botulinum Toxin Injection, Part 1 p4, which cites the German-Austrian Dysport study (Jost, Hefter, Reißig, Kollewe, Wissel). Paraphrased for the NeuroInject app. Pattern numbering (I-V) follows the original publication.

patterns.name: Pattern I
patterns.summary: Classic UE flexor-synergy posture with supination
patterns.postureDescription: Internally rotated and adducted shoulder; flexed elbow; supinated forearm; flexed wrist.
patterns.clinicalNotes: One of the most common UE patterns after stroke. Supination (rather than pronation) distinguishes this from Pattern IV.

patterns.name: Pattern II
patterns.postureDescription: Internally rotated and adducted shoulder; flexed elbow; supinated forearm; extended wrist.
patterns.clinicalNotes: Uncommon variant. The extended-wrist component may reflect extensor overactivity or a compensatory posture rather than a true spastic pattern.

patterns.name: Pattern III
patterns.postureDescription: Internally rotated and adducted shoulder; flexed elbow; neutral forearm; neutral wrist.
patterns.clinicalNotes: Distal joints are spared — treatment focuses on shoulder and elbow flexors. Common in milder presentations or after earlier distal recovery.

patterns.name: Pattern IV
patterns.summary: Classic UE flexor-synergy with pronation (most common)
patterns.postureDescription: Internally rotated and adducted shoulder; flexed elbow; pronated forearm; flexed wrist.
patterns.clinicalNotes: The most common UE pattern after stroke. Pronation distinguishes it from Pattern I. Pronator teres is a primary treatment target in this pattern.

patterns.name: Pattern V
patterns.postureDescription: Internally rotated shoulder with retroversion (pushed back); extended elbow; pronated forearm; flexed wrist.
patterns.clinicalNotes: The rarest pattern — the elbow is extended, not flexed. Usually indicates predominant triceps spasticity, which requires different treatment planning than the flexor-dominant Patterns I-IV.

handTypes.name: Spastic Flexion Hand
handTypes.description: Fingers and wrist held in flexion — the fist is closed and often cannot be opened without force. Driven by overactivity of the long finger and wrist flexors (FDS, FDP, FCR, FCU).

handTypes.name: Claw Hand
handTypes.summary: Intrinsic-minus posture — MCP extension with IP flexion
handTypes.description: Metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joints are hyperextended while interphalangeal (IP) joints are flexed. Caused by relative weakness of the hand intrinsics (lumbricals, interossei) with preserved or overactive long flexors and extensors.
handTypes._noteOnMissingMuscles: Extensor digitorum is also a key contributor to claw hand but is not yet in NeuroInject's muscle library. Add this field once it is included.

handTypes.name: Lumbrical Spasticity Hand
handTypes.summary: Intrinsic-plus posture — MCP flexion with IP extension
handTypes.description: Opposite of claw hand. MCP joints are flexed while IP joints are extended. Driven by overactivity of the lumbricals and interossei. Uncommon but distinctive — reserve lumbrical-focused injection for this clear pattern.
